newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open unch before home sales data.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open unch before home sales data.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries opened unchanged on Monday ahead of a mid-morning report on March single-family home sales and facing four key economic reports later this week.
The conclusion of the weekend G7 meeting had little impact on Treasuries, analysts said.

The 30-year bond was at 93-20/32, unchanged from Friday, with its yield at 7.14 percent. Five-year notes were unchanged at 99-04/32, yielding 6.83 percent, and 10-year notes were unchanged at 95-4/32, yielding 6.94 percent.

The only economic report the market will get during this trading session will be on March new home sales. Economists polled by Reuters said that those data, due at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT, are likely to show that sales of new single-family homes occurred at a seasonally adjusted annualized rate of 794,000 in March, down from an 811,000 seasonally adjusted annualized rate in February.
But the weight of the market's attention is now directed at economic data to be released during the rest of the week, participants said.

They said the market feared that the data, beginning with Tuesday's release of the first-quarter Employment Cost Index (ECI), would emphasize a robust economy and push the Federal Reserve closer to instituting another interest-rate hike at its May 20 policy meeting.
After a 0.8 percent fourth-quarter gain, the ECI is likely to be up 0.9 percent for the first quarter of 1997, economists told Reuters.
A 1.0-percent rise or more would lead the markets to expect another Fed rate hike, traders said. But a rise of just 0.8 percent could provoke a "relief" rally, they said.

Other key data set for release later this week include the first-quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP), expected to be up 4.1 percent, the April National Association of Purchasing Management's (NAPM) index, and the government's payroll employment data for April.

Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A., said the March single family home sales data due at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT on Monday were likely to be overshadowed by economic reports due later in the week.
"You'd have to get a significant change in sales to attract any interest," he said.
Awareness of the ECI, GDP, NAPM and payrolls data due this week also restrained any potential Treasury market reaction to the G-7 meeting, Stiles said.

"The G-7 firmed up the dollar but the reaction didn't spill over into the Treasury market," he said. "The Treasury market sees the dollar but also realizes that intervention is a possibility. But even more important, the main interest for the Treasury market is seeing the big data this week."
Stiles said if Tuesday's Q1 ECI report came in at 0.8 percent, below the market's consensus 0.9 percent estimate, "there will be a relief rally for sure."
A 0.9 percent Q1 ECI would be inconclusive for the market, Stiles said.

Meanwhile, the market is in a range-trading, wait-and-see mode with resistance stationed at 107-13/32, the 20-day moving average on the June T-bond contract, Stiles said. Support for the market is located at 106-20/32, he said.
In morning trade, two-year notes were unchanged at 99-22/32, yielding 6.54 percent.
Six-month and year bill rates were also unchanged at 5.40 percent and 5.74 percent, respectively. Three-month bill rates were edged up one basis point to 5.17 percent.
